claims.text: The tested HfNbTiVAl10 is in an as-processed hierarchical heterostructure state at room temperature.
HfNbTiVAl10 has characteristic mesoscale heterogeneities and interfacial features.
High-speed DIC can measure evolving strain fields during tensile testing.
Combined high-speed DIC and synchrotron imaging can capture strain localization, crack initiation, and crack propagation across the hierarchical microstructure.
Real-time imaging data can be fed into a multiscale simulation and used for dynamic recalibration during the test.
Locally evolving strain heterogeneities and crack propagation govern the tensile mechanical response of the hierarchical heterostructure.
Real-time imaging quantifies local strain distributions and crack dynamics.
Continuous imaging-based recalibration enables more rapid model convergence.
Continuous imaging-based recalibration improves the accuracy of predicted mechanical properties.
The framework will predict Young's modulus with no more than 5% error relative to independent measurements.
The framework will predict yield strength with no more than 5% error relative to independent measurements.
The framework will predict fracture characteristics with no more than 5% error relative to independent measurements.
The framework can provide predictions up to seven times faster than established simulation approaches.
Conventional simulations use static, steady-state calibration and omit dynamic local strain variation and crack initiation.
Established atomistic simulation approaches face length-, time-, and wall-clock limitations when modeling experimentally relevant deformation rates.
Failure to represent dynamic local strain variation or crack initiation causes conventional simulations to be less accurate.
Insufficient imaging rate at high strain rates may prevent rapid strain evolution from being captured.
Imaging noise or calibration drift may produce significant discrepancies between predicted and measured outcomes.
Young's modulus and yield strength can be obtained from measured stress-strain curves.
The hypothesis is predeclared as falsified if predicted strain fields differ by more than 10% from imaging measurements or if any specified mechanical-property prediction error exceeds 5%.
